catalog_quote: p. 61 (§2.2.1 TONE): "Ekegusii, like most Bantu languages, is a tone language" ... "The domain of tone in Ekegusii is the word and units that bear it are vowels." p. 64 (§2.2.2 STRESS): "Studies that have been carried out on Bantu languages reveal that primary stress occurs on the penultimate sysllable [sic]. However, there is no clear distinction that categorizes the kind of stress found in these languages into secondary and tertiary stresses." p. 65: "In Ekegusii, prominence tends to occur on the radical if this is of a shape vc,cvc, cvvc, cv and on the syllable of long radicals. In such longer radicals there may be a subsidiary prominence on the final syllable." ... "Given the scope of this work, a lot may not be said on these two aspects of Ekegusii phonology. A thorough investigation needs to be done on the suprasegmental elements of the language which perhaps will bring out clear distinctions of stress and prominence." p. 66: "The only observable feature that should be noted is that stress occurs on the penultimate syllable for which we formulate the following rule to show stress acquisition. 10) [+syllable] --> [+stress] / ___ (C) V#" (rule (10) read from the rendered page image; the text garbles it).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Gusii (gusi1247) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's only keyword-title item, Philippson 1991 (Paris 5 thesis on tone and accent in East African Bantu), has no online text (theses.fr 'accessible: non'; not in HAL); its abstract places ~30 languages on a continuum from fully tonal to penultimate demarcative stress but does not name Gusii, so its Gusii content is unverified (priority medium). Searching the University of Nairobi repository turned up an open first-hand statement: Osinde 1988 (MA, UoN), §2.2.2 pp. 64–66, says Ekegusii is a tone language and that 'stress occurs on the penultimate syllable' (rule 10), while 'prominence' tends to fall on the verb radical; the author calls the treatment preliminary. Three Komenda intonation works (2020, 2022, 2023 PhD, all read) confirm Ekegusii is a tone language with lexically contrastive H/L but say nothing about word-stress placement; Bickmore 1998, Nyauma 2016 and Ingonga 1991 are silent. The likely best source, Cammenga 2002 (Köppe reference grammar), is print/HathiTrust search-only (priority high); Nash 2011 (UCSB tone dissertation) is ProQuest-paywalled (priority medium).fr, IDEALS and HathiTrust catalog APIs. with.

Title page: "Ekegusii Morphophonology: An Analysis of the Major Consonantal Processes", Osinde Ken Nyauncho, MA dissertation, Dept. of Linguistics and African Languages, University of Nairobi, June 1988 (open UoN eRepository PDF). All four quoted passages are on the page scan verbatim; one locator is off: "Ekegusii, like most Bantu languages, is a tone language" is at §2.2.1 TONE on printed p. 61 (p. 76), not p. 63 (p. 78) as the compiler stated. §2.2.2 STRESS pp. 64-66 = pp. 79-81 is correct: p. 64 "Studies that have been carried out on Bantu languages reveal that primary stress occurs on the penultimate sysllable [sic, typed o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ekegusii is a tone language (H, L, falling); word stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable by rule. A distinct 'prominence' (loudness/duration/F0) tends to fall on the verb radical, with a subsidiary prominence on the final syllable of long radicals.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author says the Bantu literature gives 'no clear distinction' of secondary and tertiary stress (p. 64); the only graded remark is a 'subsidiary prominence on the final syllable' of long radicals (p. 65).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Separately, 'prominence' (perceived loudness: duration, F0, amplitude) 'tends to occur on the radical' for radicals of shape VC, CVC, CVVC, CV, with a 'subsidiary prominence on the final syllable' of long radicals (p. 65). The author cautions that little can be said within the scope of the work and that a thorough investigation of the suprasegmentals is still needed (pp. 65-66); the opening sentence generalises from Bantu studies rather than from Ekegusii data.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the rule is stated for stress 'on the penultimate syllable' of the word (rule 10, p. 66) with no phrase-level qualification and no mention of citation vs. connected forms; the 'prominence' remarks concern the verb radical. Hyman & Nyamwaro 2023 (fn. 4, 8) treat penultimate prominence and the ban on final H:-L as phrase-based, so the penult effects are probably phrase-final in connected speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Osinde 1988 describes Ekegusii generally (states the language 'shows little dialectal variation', no dialect named); the statement is for gusi1247 as a whole, not a specific dialect (Rogoro/Maate).

In such longer radicals there may be a subsidiary prominence on the final syllable." p. 66: "The only observable feature that should be noted is that stress occurs on the penultimate syllable for which we formulate the following rule to show stress acquisition."

new_statements.reading: Ekegusii is described as a tone language (H/L, plus falling), and word stress is placed on the penultimate syllable by a stress-assignment rule (rule 10, p. 66; its formalism is garbled in the PDF text). Osinde distinguishes this from 'prominence', which tends to sit on the verb radical (root) with a subsidiary prominence on the final syllable of long radicals, and he flags the whole suprasegmental section as preliminary. Reading for a catalog: fixed penultimate stress in a tone language, from a single MA-level first-hand source; Cammenga 2002 (unread, print/HathiTrust search-only) should be checked before this classification is relied on.

tone_statements.citation: Nyaboga, Linet Bichang'a; Otieno, Peter Nyansera; Mecha, Evans Gesura. 2026. The Interaction of Obstruent Features and Tone in Ekegusii. East African Journal of Arts and Social Sciences 9(3): 775-791. doi:10.37284/eajass.9.3.5781 (CC BY 4.0).
tone_statements.quote: The Ekegusii data indicate that this perturbation operates alongside, rather than replaces, lexical tone. Although the language employs tonal contrasts to distinguish lexical meaning, the acoustic realisation of those tonal targets is significantly conditioned by the laryngeal properties of preceding consonants. The higher onset frequencies observed after voiceless obstruents gradually converge toward the intended tonal target as the vowel progresses, illustrating the interaction between intrinsic phonetic effects and phonological tone.

tone_statements.summary: Acoustic Praat study: treats Ekegusii as a lexical tone language whose tonal targets are perturbed by obstruent voicing and prenasalisation; gives no tone inventory, TBU or tone-marked forms.

tone_statements.quote: As seen, H(igh) tone is marked by an acute accent (´) and L(ow) tone is unmarked. Many Bantu languages are analyzed with a privative /H/ vs. Ø tone contrast rather than /H/ vs. /L/. This is the case in Konda as well as Ekegusii (§2). … Turning to tone, verb roots can be either toneless, e.g. /-sibor-/ ‘untie’ or have a /H/ on their first mora, e.g. /-súgum-/ ‘push’. … As elsewhere, toneless moras receive a default L(ow) tone. In Tone Pattern II (TPII), a suffixal or “melodic” H tone is assigned from the second to final moras of the verb stem

sources.citation: Komenda, Samwel (2023). Intonation in Ekegusii, Its Interaction with Information Structure and How It Is Perceived by Native Speakers. PhD thesis, University of Nairobi. 393 pp.
sources.quote: As already pointed out, Ekegusii is a tone language. This means that the language uses tone for making lexical and grammatical contrasts. This use of tone in Ekegusii has been described in Whiteley (1960), Bickmore (1999), Cammenga (2002), Elwell (2008) and Nash (2011). [...] Cammenga (2002) commenting on Whiteley's work notes that to a limited extent it is only the high and low tones that are lexically distinctive in Ekegusii.
sources.note: Intonation study (ToBI/PRAAT). Treats Ekegusii as a tone language (H/L lexically contrastive, falling tones attested), explicitly contrasted with 'stress languages' like English; reports an upstepped H on the penultimate syllable as a yes–no question cue. No statement of word-stress placement.

sources.citation: Komenda, Samwel; Oduor, Jane A. N; Jerono, Prisca (2022). Differences of age and gender in pitch range modulation in yes-no questions in Ekegusii.
sources.quote: Phonologically, this implies that Ekegusii yes-no questions do not end in a final high (H%) boundary tone which is a common feature in yes–no interrogatives in stress languages like English (Sadat-Tehrani, 2007: 70).
sources.note: Question intonation; contrasts Ekegusii (tonal) with stress languages; silent on word-stress placement.

sources.note: Tone paper (privative /H/ vs. toneless; grammatical H mapping). No word-stress statement. sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
